These exercises let you practise the verbs from the *Data Analysis 2* part of the course book: `filter()`, `mutate()`, `summarise()`, and `group_by()`. They all use the same `titanic_df` dataset from the course, but ask different questions from the examples in the book, so you'll need to adapt what you've learned.

Write your code in the box, then click **Run Code** to see the result and get feedback.

The last two exercises are a bit more of a stretch - come back to them once you're comfortable with the rest.

## Exercise 1: `filter()` with one condition

Filter `titanic_df` to keep only the passengers who **did not survive**. The `survived` column is `1` for passengers who survived and `0` for those who didn't.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_1
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_1
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_1" }
Use `filter()` on the `survived` column. To check whether two things are equal, use a double equals sign: `==`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_1" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_1
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> filter(survived == 0)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_1
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "That's it - the 809 passengers who did not survive.")
  fail("Not quite. Check you're using a double equals sign (==) and the right number for passengers who didn't survive.")
})
```

## Exercise 2: `filter()` with a numeric condition

Filter `titanic_df` to keep only passengers who were **60 or older**.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_2
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_2
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_2" }
"60 or older" includes 60 itself. `>` means "greater than"; `>=` means "greater than or equal to".
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_2" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_2
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> filter(age >= 60)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_2
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "Correct - the 40 passengers aged 60 or over.")
  fail("Not quite. Make sure passengers who were exactly 60 are included.")
})
```

## Exercise 3: combining conditions with `&`

Filter `titanic_df` to keep only **male** passengers who embarked at **Queenstown** (`embarked` is `'Q'`).

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_3
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_3
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_3" }
You need two conditions that must both be true: one on `sex`, one on `embarked`. Join them with `&`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_3" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_3
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> filter(sex == 'male' & embarked == 'Q')
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_3
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "That's it - men who boarded at Queenstown.")
  fail("Not quite. Both conditions must be true at once - check you're using & and that the text values are in quotes.")
})
```

## Exercise 4: combining conditions with `|`

Two columns record family on board: `sibsp` (number of siblings or spouses) and `parch` (number of parents or children). Filter `titanic_df` to keep passengers travelling with **any** family: those with at least one sibling or spouse, **or** at least one parent or child.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_4
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_4
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_4" }
"At least one" means greater than 0. Use `|` so that a row is kept if either condition is true.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_4" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_4
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> filter(sibsp > 0 | parch > 0)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_4
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "Correct - the 519 passengers travelling with family.")
  fail("Not quite. Remember | means 'at least one of these is true', which is different to &.")
})
```

## Exercise 5: `%in%`

Use `%in%` to filter `titanic_df` to keep only passengers in **second or third class** (`pclass` is 2 or 3).

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_5
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_5
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_5" }
`%in%` checks whether a value is in a list you give it, like `c(2, 3)`. Because these are numbers, they don't need quotation marks.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_5" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_5
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> filter(pclass %in% c(2, 3))
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_5
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "That's it - second and third class passengers.")
  fail("Not quite. Check you're using %in% on the pclass column, with both class numbers.")
})
```

## Exercise 6: `mutate()`

Create a new column called `family_size`: the number of people in each passenger's family group on board. Add `sibsp` and `parch` together, then add 1 for the passenger themselves.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_6
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_6
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_6" }
Inside `mutate()`, give the new column name, then `=`, then the calculation. You can add columns together with `+`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_6" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_6
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> mutate(family_size = sibsp + parch + 1)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_6
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "That's it - a new family_size column.")
  fail("Not quite. Check the column name is exactly family_size, and that you've added 1 for the passenger.")
})
```

## Exercise 7: `mutate()` with `if_else()`

Create a new column called `travelling`, which is `'alone'` if the passenger had no siblings, spouses, parents or children on board (`sibsp + parch` is 0), and `'with family'` otherwise.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_7
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_7
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_7" }
`if_else()` takes three things: a condition, the value if it's true, and the value if it's false. You can do a calculation inside the condition, for example `sibsp + parch == 0`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_7" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_7
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> mutate(travelling = if_else(sibsp + parch == 0, 'alone', 'with family'))
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_7
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "Correct - 790 passengers travelled alone and 519 with family.")
  fail("Not quite. Check the condition, and the exact spelling of 'alone' and 'with family'.")
})
```

## Exercise 8: `summarise()`

In a single `summarise()`, calculate the age of the **youngest** passenger, calling it `youngest`, and the **median** fare, calling it `median_fare`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_8
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_8
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_8" }
Look at the list of summary functions in the `summarise()` chapter: `min()` and `median()` will help. Some ages and one fare are missing, so add `na.rm = TRUE` to each.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_8" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_8
#| solution: true
titanic_df |> summarise(youngest = min(age, na.rm = TRUE), median_fare = median(fare, na.rm = TRUE))
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_8
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "That's it. The youngest passenger was about two months old (0.17 years), and the median fare was 14.45.")
  fail("Not quite. Check your column names match exactly, and don't forget na.rm = TRUE in both functions.")
})
```

## Stretch exercise 9: `group_by()` and `summarise()`

For each port of embarkation (`embarked`), calculate the number of passengers (call it `passengers`) and the share who survived (call it `survival`). Did it matter where you got on?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_9
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_9
titanic_df |>
  ______ |>
  ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_9" }
Group by `embarked`. Because `survived` is 1 or 0, its mean is the share who survived (see "women and children first" in the grouping chapter). Use `n()` for the count and `mean(survived)` for the share.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_9" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_9
#| solution: true
titanic_df |>
  group_by(embarked) |>
  summarise(passengers = n(), survival = mean(survived))
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_9
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "Great work. 56% of Cherbourg passengers survived, against 33% from Southampton. Why might that be? Try grouping by pclass as well.")
  fail("Not quite. Check you're grouping by embarked, and that both summary columns are named and calculated correctly.")
})
```

## Stretch exercise 10: `mutate()` with `case_when()`

Create a new column called `fare_band`, with **three** categories based on `fare`: `'low'` for under 10, `'medium'` for 10 up to (but not including) 50, and `'high'` for 50 and over.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10
#| setup: true
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yann-ryan/infovis-course/master/titanic_df_full.csv"
download.file(url, "titanic_df.csv")
titanic_df <- read_csv("titanic_df.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10
titanic_df |> ______
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_10" }
`case_when()` takes a series of `condition ~ value` pairs, checked in order. It stops at the first match, so you don't need to repeat `fare >= 10` for the middle band:

```r
mutate(fare_band = case_when(
  fare < 10 ~ "low",
  fare < 50 ~ "medium",
  fare >= 50 ~ "high"
))
```
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_10" }
#### Solution

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10
#| solution: true
titanic_df |>
  mutate(fare_band = case_when(
    fare < 10 ~ "low",
    fare < 50 ~ "medium",
    fare >= 50 ~ "high"
  ))
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this({
  pass_if_equal(explanation = "Excellent - all three fare bands, correctly assigned. (One passenger has no fare recorded, so their band is NA.)")
  fail("Not quite there yet. Check each of the three fare boundaries carefully, and the exact spelling of each category.")
})
```
